newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: U.S. NATO nod signals Czech stability-govt.
newsitem.headline: U.S. NATO nod signals Czech stability-govt.

text.p: The Prague government said on Thursday the U.S. selection of the Czech Republic as a preferred candidate for NATO expansion was a clear sign of the country's stability, despite some recent setbacks.

"The government of the Czech Republic welcomes today's announcement by President Clinton... as an evaluation of the stable development of our country until now," said a statement issued on behalf of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus.

In the first definitive naming of its preferences for NATO expansion, the Clinton administration said it thought that only the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland should be invited to join in a first round of new members.

The statement came two days after the government narrowly survived a confidence vote after a sharp drop in the Czech crown brought on by poor macroeconomic results and cracks within the ruling centre-right alliance.
In a clear attempt to reassure potential NATO partners, the government promised to assume all responsibilities of NATO membership.
"The Czech Republic is prepared to bear all obligations and costs connected with the country's full membership in NATO," the statement said.
It said NATO expansion offered an historic opportunity to anchor Prague definitively in the Euro-Atlantic community while providing "so necessary security guarantees."
The Czech people have been lukewarm to joining NATO after four decades under Soviet domination in the Warsaw Pact.
A poll in May by the state-run agency IVVM said 45 percent of adult Czechs favoured NATO membership, up from 42 percent in April, while 34 percent were opposed and 21 percent were undecided.

The Czech government has been struggling to find the money to upgrade its Soviet-era equipment with NATO-compatible weapons. The will to buy advanced Western fighter planes has still not found the wallet.
The Czech plane maker Aero a.s. on Thursday unveiled its new L-159 fighter, an upgrade of a Soviet-era design using U.S. technology. The Czech army is due to receive 72 of the new planes.
Boeing Co unit Rockwell International provided the avionics for the L-159, while the engines came from Allied Signal Aerospace and components from other Western suppliers.
The Czech army says its command and control structure has been fully reformed from its Cold War officer-driven organisation to a force answerable to a democratically-elected government.
